rounds.proof_sketch: K=32 and tile_size=32, so tile iterations = (32+31)/32 = 1. The removed __syncthreads() at line 55 is at the END of the tile loop. Its purpose is to prevent race conditions between iteration i's reads and iteration i+1's writes. With exactly 1 iteration, there is no 'next iteration' that would overwrite shared memory while other threads are still reading. Therefore, the sync is redundant under this fixed configuration.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation removes the second __syncthreads() at the end of the tile loop. This synchronization barrier is designed to ensure that all threads finish reading from shared memory (A_tile, B_tile) before any thread begins writing new tile data in the next iteration. However, with K=32 and a tile size of 32, there is exactly ONE tile iteration: (K+31)/32 = (32+31)/32 = 1. After the single iteration's computation completes (reading from shared memory), the loop exits immediately - no thread ever writes to shared memory again. Since no write-after-read hazard can occur when there's only one iteration, the barrier is semantically unnecessary. The EMD Layer 2 evidence showing bitwise equivalence across 112 test rounds confirms this analysis.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed configuration. The mutation would only be killable if K > 32 (requiring multiple tile iterations), but K=32 is fixed. No value-level input can trigger the race condition because the race requires multiple loop iterations, not particular data values.
rounds.recommendations: When testing sync-removal mutations in tiled GPU kernels, verify whether the number of tile iterations is 1 (making end-of-loop syncs redundant) or >1 (where races become possible). Include test configurations with varying tile counts to catch sync-related bugs. For mutation testing, consider the loop trip count as a key factor in sync barrier necessity.
